label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
Here it is. I kept your voice — the anger is in there, but I took the insults out so the whole thing lands harder. In English, for his wife to read, but it still sounds like you talking.

Four blanks to fill in if you want: **[his wife's name]**, **[the agent's name]**, **[the date the listing went up]**, and **[when your rent goes up / the developer's name]**, if you know it.

---

**Subject: The building on rue Saint-Hubert — please call me**

Denis,

I am writing this from the back room of the shop. I have started it four times. The first three came out half in French and full of things I would be ashamed of if you read them, so I am starting again, in English, for your wife, and I am going to try to say this like a reasonable person who is very, very angry.

Let me start with Thursday.

Thursday, six in the morning, I was shaping baguettes. A man walked into my shop with a camera and a tripod. He said he was the photographer for the agency. He said Mr. Denis had told him it was fine, that you had told him I was okay with it, that I knew about it.

I knew nothing.

Karine had to take me in the back and get me to sit down. Karine, who works for me, who has worked for me for eleven years, was the one holding me together at six in the morning while a stranger set up his lights in front of my ovens. That is what you did. You did not even pick up the phone. You sent a photographer into my shop to tell me my father's building was for sale — the building where I have worked every single day for thirty-one years.

Then I found it on Centris. Your name on it. Three-storey, rue Saint-Hubert. Asking $1,150,000.

I need you to read what you actually did there. Not what you meant to do. What you did.

---

Let me tell you what that building is, since it seems to have become a number on a listing sheet.

Papa bought it in 1979. Three floors, the bakery on the ground, two apartments above. I was twenty-six years old. I had nothing, you had nothing, and he put his name on the deed and he signed it and he handed me the keys to the shop and he said *go*. Do you remember the back room? The room with the flour sacks in it, where we slept when we were kids because there was no other place for us. Papa let you sleep in the flour sacks room because you loved it. You told that story at every single family dinner for twenty years. You still tell it. That is the same building, Denis. That is the same room with the sacks in it.

And since maman died in February, and the estate settled in August, that building has been half yours and half mine. Since August I have been paying $2,400 a month to the estate. Not once late. Not once, in eleven months. I can show you every deposit, every receipt, if you want to see them. And in 2019 I paid $38,000 for the new roof on that building myself, out of my own pocket, because it was leaking and nobody was going to fix it and I was not going to argue with a man who was sick. I have never asked anyone for that money back. I am not asking now either. I am telling you what it costs me because it seems like nobody has been counting.

---

Now let me tell you what I did, before you tell me I ambushed you.

In September, I called you. Like I always call you. And I told you: I want to buy your half. I told you the caisse had already pre-approved me for $410,000. I told you that on the phone, Denis, out loud, with a number. And you said we would talk about it. And then nothing. Nothing for months.

And then — three weeks after maman's funeral — you called me yourself. You said: *"No rush, we decide together."*

Ensemble. Together. I wrote it down, Denis. I wrote it on the back of a delivery invoice, because I was holding a phone and a pen and I wanted to remember that you said it.

You said *together* to me, and then you listed the building behind my back with an agent, and the first person to tell me was a man with a camera in my shop at six in the morning.

Do you understand the word? Together means I am in the room when the decision is made. Together means you call me and you say "Denis wants to sell, here is what I am thinking," and I get to argue, and we end up somewhere, and afterwards we are still brothers. That is what together means. What you did was not together. What you did was *done*. You decided alone, and then you made a photographer the messenger, because calling your sister was harder than sending a stranger.

---

And now the business, since you think I am being sentimental.

You are right that I am sentimental. I am sentimental about the flour sacks room. I will be sentimental about it until I die. But this is not sentiment, this is arithmetic.

The asking price is $1,150,000. Your half of that number is $575,000. My pre-approval is $410,000. There is $165,000 between us, and it is not there because I am a baker and not a businessman. It is there because $1,150,000 is a developer's number for a building he wants to see torn down. My half, the half with six employees and thirty-one years of clients in it, is worth $410,000 to the bank that knows my bread and my payroll and my name for twenty-six years.

But I am not going to sit here and tell you I cannot buy you out. Here is what I can do, and I am offering it in writing:

- I can take the whole building, apartments and all, and take your half over time. Vendor take-back mortgage, ten or twelve years, at a rate the caisse will accept, with the two apartments as security.
- Or we sell the two apartments separately and split the money.
- Or we get a real appraisal from a broker you trust, not the man who is photographing my shop, and we price the building like a building.
- Or, if you want the whole thing sold tomorrow, you sell it to me at the appraisal with a take-back.

Any of those. All of them are normal things that normal people do. What is not normal is a photographer at six in the morning.

Here is what happens if nobody stops this. There is a developer. He is going to tear it down or turn it into condos, and my rent is going to double, and my lease ends on 30 April 2027, and I will be out on the sidewalk with six employees and no building. I cannot survive that. I am not being dramatic — I am fifty-seven years old, this is my life, and it is the only business I have ever had. Six people work for me. Their families eat because this bakery is open. My clients have been buying bread from me since 1995 and they know my name and I know theirs and I know what Mrs. Bouchard buys on Saturdays.

If they double my rent I close. That is the math. You can price the building with the bakery in it or you can price it like an empty lot with a future tower on it, and if you price it the second way, you are not selling a building, you are selling my bakery to a man with a crane.

---

I am not going to pretend I am not furious. I have been furious since Thursday. I have been up at five every morning anyway, because the bread does not care how I feel and neither do my customers.

But I want to say this part clearly, because it is the part that matters.

It was not the price that hurt me. It was the manner. If you had called me on Thursday — even if you had called me and said "Denis, I want to sell, I am listing it on Monday, and you are going to hate it" — I would have been hurt. But I would have heard it from my brother. Instead I heard it from a stranger, in my shop, while I had flour on my hands, and then Karine had to explain to me why a photographer was there.

And you said *no rush*. You said that to me. Three weeks after maman.

I am not going to hire a lawyer over this. Not yet, and honestly not because it is the smart thing — because I would rather have my brother than I would rather be right. But I want you to know that if this is how you do business with me, I will, and you will not like what that looks like. So do not make it a lawyer.

---

So here is what I am asking, and I am asking for these three things by the end of the week:

**1. Take it off the market this week.** Friday, Saturday, whatever day it takes. I am not asking to be the only bidder. I am asking that the listing comes down while we talk, so that a photographer does not walk into my shop again and so that I can stop looking at my father's address with a price on it.

**2. If it stays on the market, give me first right to buy in writing.** Not a promise on the phone, in a message from your wife, or a handshake in your car in the parking lot of a funeral home. In writing, from you, with a deadline — thirty days before you accept any other offer, and no showings, no photographer, no agent in my shop without my written consent. Send it to me and I will have my lawyer look at it, just that one page, and I will sign it back the same day.

**3. Call me.** Not a text. Not a message relayed through your wife. I want to hear your voice on the phone and I want to hear it from you, not from Claire, because I have been talking to a photographer and an agent and a stranger and I am tired of talking to everyone except my brother.

Call me at the shop between five and seven in the morning, or at home after eight. I will pick up. I will answer.

---

Denis, I don't want to lose you. I have one brother. I am fifty-seven years old, I do not have time to build a new family, and honestly I do not want one. Maman would be sick. Papa would have taken the phone out of your hand and said, *"Denis. Pick up the phone and call your sister."* You know he would have. He would have said it in that voice he had.

So we can do this the way we should have done it in September — the two of us, on the phone, arguing about a number like we argue about everything, and then going to lunch, and then being brothers.

Call me.

I am not going to hire a lawyer. I am going to bake bread at five in the morning. And I am waiting for you to call.

**Karine says hello. She also says to tell you that the baguettes have been excellent this week, because apparently I am angrier and the dough responds to it.**

---

Want me to soften the opening, sharpen the three demands, or add a short second paragraph at the end that makes it clear you're willing to drop the listing entirely if he agrees to sell to you first? I can also cut it down to about 900 words if you'd rather he not have too much to hide behind.
